title: Manufacturing's Security Patchwork: Why Piecemeal Browser Add-ons and Manual Policies Leave Factories Exposed
excerpt: As manufacturing embraces digital transformation, traditional browser security approaches are failing to protect against sophisticated threats. This article explores why piecemeal security solutions are insufficient and how enterprise browsers can transform manufacturing security.
content:
The manufacturing industry stands at the forefront of global digital transformation, with smart factories, cloud-based workflows, and interconnected supply chains driving unprecedented productivity and innovation. Yet, as the browser becomes the primary gateway to sensitive data and operational dashboards, manufacturers continue to rely on a patchwork of security add-ons and manual policy enforcement for browser protection. This approach is increasingly outmatched by today's sophisticated cyber threats, leading to inconsistent protection, operational risk, and missed opportunities.

The Manufacturing Threat Landscape: Real-World Incidents

Recent years have seen manufacturing become a prime target for cybercriminals. In March 2025 alone, the sector suffered 91 ransomware incidents globally, with the United States being the most targeted. Attackers are leveraging automated brute-force attacks, exploiting IoT devices, and deploying ransomware-as-a-service models to bypass traditional defenses. Groups like Black Basta and Moonstone Sleet have demonstrated the ability to automate attacks and bypass legacy security measures, while new entrants such as Arkana and CrazyHunter are complicating the threat landscape further, as detailed in our analysis of manufacturing security challenges.

Manufacturing Breach Statistics and Attack Vectors

The 2025 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) reveals significant cybersecurity challenges specifically affecting the manufacturing sector. According to the report, malware presence in manufacturing breaches has risen dramatically to 66% in 2025, representing a substantial increase that underscores the sector's vulnerability to sophisticated cyber attacks. Ransomware continues to be a dominant threat, accounting for nearly half (47%) of those malware incidents. Hacking via stolen credentials (34%), exploiting vulnerabilities (23%), and phishing (19%) are also common attack vectors, as reported by Industrial Cyber.

Financial Impact on Manufacturing Organizations

The financial consequences of data breaches in manufacturing are substantial and continue to escalate. According to the IBM 2022 Cost of a Data Breach Report, the average data breach cost for manufacturing firms reached $4.47 million, representing a 5.4% increase from 2021. This places manufacturing among the industries with higher-than-average breach costs, reflecting the unique challenges these organizations face in terms of operational downtime, supply chain disruption, and regulatory compliance requirements.

Additionally, the 2024 IBM Cost of a Data Breach report shows that industrial organizations (including manufacturing) faced an average breach cost of $5.56 million, reflecting an 18% increase compared to 2023.

Emerging Threat: Browser-Native Ransomware

One of the most concerning developments in the current threat landscape is the emergence of browser-native ransomware, a novel attack methodology that represents a significant evolution in cybercriminal tactics. Unlike traditional ransomware that requires victims to download malicious files, browser-native ransomware operates entirely within web browsers, targeting victims' digital identities to gain unauthorized access to cloud-based file storage, email systems, and password repositories.

This attack methodology is particularly insidious because it completely bypasses traditional endpoint security solutions. Research from SquareX has documented how these attacks leverage artificial intelligence agents to systematically exfiltrate files and sensitive data stored in Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) applications, threatening to leak this information unless ransom demands are met, as reported by Cyber Risk Leaders and SiliconANGLE.

Why Traditional Security Falls Short

The Patchwork Approach

Manufacturers often rely on standard browsers like Chrome or Edge, deploying them via tools such as the Google Chrome Enterprise Installer, MSI, or web download. To compensate for browser risks, they add a mix of security extensions, manual group policies, and endpoint security agents. While these tools offer some protection, they create a fragmented security environment that is:

  • Difficult to manage: Each add-on or policy must be updated and configured separately, increasing IT overhead.
  • Inconsistent: Security gaps emerge as users disable extensions, ignore updates, or apply settings incorrectly.
  • Reactive: Most add-ons detect threats after they occur, rather than proactively blocking them.
  • Limited in scope: Many threats, such as browser-native ransomware or malicious OAuth apps, slip through traditional endpoint defenses.

Real-World Consequences

The limitations of this patchwork approach have led to significant incidents:

  • Ransomware outbreaks: During the 2025 surge in ransomware attacks, many manufacturers fell victim to exploits that bypassed endpoint security by targeting browsers directly.
  • Supply chain disruption: Attackers have used browser-based phishing and credential theft to move laterally from IT to OT networks, disrupting production and stealing intellectual property.
  • Insider threats: Malicious or careless employees can exfiltrate sensitive data or introduce malware through browser-based interfaces, especially when extensions or manual policies are inconsistently enforced.

The Case for an Enterprise Browser

An enterprise browser is purpose-built for business environments, offering integrated security, management, and productivity features that go far beyond what consumer browsers and add-ons can provide. As detailed in our analysis of enterprise browser adoption trends, these specialized browsers are rapidly transforming how organizations approach web security. Unlike the patchwork approach, an enterprise browser like Oasis by Kahana offers:

  • Zero Trust Security Architecture: Every session requires continuous identity verification and least-privilege access, so even if an attacker gains access, they can't move laterally or escalate privileges without real-time checks.
  • Granular Permission and Content Security Policies: Strict controls limit resource loading to trusted sources and block unauthorized scripts, frames, or form submissions—protecting against cross-site scripting (XSS), clickjacking, and browser-based exploits.
  • Advanced Certificate and Mixed Content Management: Robust SSL/TLS validation ensures all connections are encrypted, and automatic HTTPS enforcement blocks attackers from injecting malicious content.
  • Comprehensive Permission Management: Administrators can apply a default-deny policy to sensitive browser features such as camera, microphone, clipboard, and downloads, managed on a per-origin basis.
  • Real-Time Threat Detection and Content Filtering: Built-in threat intelligence blocks access to known phishing sites, malicious downloads, and suspicious URLs in real time.
  • Centralized Management and Audit Capabilities: IT teams can deploy, update, and manage Oasis across the enterprise using familiar workflows, with centralized policy controls, audit logging, and compliance reporting for complete visibility.
  • Seamless User Experience and Productivity: Built on Chromium, Oasis ensures compatibility with modern web applications and a familiar interface for users transitioning from Chrome or Edge.

Workforce Enablement and Productivity

Manufacturing teams need secure, uninterrupted access to digital tools—whether on the shop floor, in engineering, or working remotely. Oasis supports workforce enablement by:

  • Providing secure remote access to internal and cloud-based resources, supporting hybrid work and third-party collaboration.
  • Offering browser for enterprise productivity with AI-powered tab grouping, project-based organization, and distraction-free focus modes.
  • Reducing reliance on virtual desktops (VDI): Unlike VDI, which is costly and complex, Oasis enables secure access to applications without performance penalties.

Real-World Impact: Preventing and Mitigating Attacks

Oasis has proven effective in preventing various types of attacks:

  • Phishing and OAuth attacks: In a standard browser, an employee might grant access to a fake productivity tool, exposing critical data. Oasis's granular permission controls and real-time threat detection would flag and block the suspicious request before damage occurs.
  • HMI vulnerabilities: Attackers exploiting browser-based human-machine interface (HMI) vulnerabilities can disrupt production lines or steal data. Oasis's strict CSP enforcement and automatic HTTPS upgrades prevent malicious scripts from executing, while centralized monitoring enables rapid response.
  • Browser-native ransomware: During the 2025 ransomware surge, organizations using Oasis benefited from reduced attack surfaces, proactive threat blocking, and the ability to quickly update security policies across all endpoints—minimizing downtime and financial loss.

Enterprise Browser Management: Why Centralization Matters

With Oasis, IT teams can enforce security policies, monitor browser activity, and deploy updates from a single dashboard. This eliminates the inconsistencies of manual policy enforcement and ensures that every user, device, and session is protected by enterprise-grade browser security—no matter where they are.

Deciding on an Enterprise Browser: Key Use Cases

Manufacturers should consider an enterprise browser for several critical scenarios:

  • Secure access for contractors and third parties: Enable safe collaboration without exposing core systems.
  • Browser extension security: Block risky or unauthorized extensions that can introduce vulnerabilities.
  • Data loss prevention: Prevent sensitive information from being copied, pasted, or downloaded to unauthorized locations.
  • Regulatory compliance: Automate audit logging and reporting to meet industry standards.

The Future of Browser Security in Manufacturing

As browser-native ransomware and identity attacks become more sophisticated, the need for secure enterprise browsers like Oasis will only grow. Manufacturing's unique combination of legacy systems, minimal downtime tolerance, and interconnected supply chains makes it especially vulnerable to browser-based threats. By adopting a secure web browser with zero-trust architecture, granular policy controls, and real-time threat intelligence, manufacturers can protect their operations, intellectual property, and reputation.

Conclusion

Manufacturing stands at a crossroads: embrace the productivity and agility of cloud-based workflows, or risk falling behind in a rapidly evolving market. But with this digital transformation comes a new wave of browser-based threats that traditional security tools and piecemeal add-ons cannot address. Real-world incidents—from high-profile ransomware attacks to sophisticated phishing campaigns—demonstrate the urgent need for a secure enterprise browser built for the realities of today's threat landscape.
